title: RCC RefCert: A Research Toolkit for Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity
description:
RCC RefCert is an open-source toolkit for studying quantum circuit complexity. Given the parameters of your preparation model, you can compute a rigorous lower bound on optimal quantum circuit complexity from final-state data. Use the target state's exact spectrum or counts collected under a prespecified measurement protocol.

You can build your own quantum models and compare preparation strategies. With a density matrix, you can study how complexity is distributed across the subsystems of a pure or mixed state. Share the model, inputs and results for independent verification.

The toolkit is based on Reference-Contingent Complexity (RCC), introduced by Liu, Tian and Wu in Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity: An Auditable Information-Theoretic Lower Bound.

Features of reference-contingent complexity

Structural fairness makes circuit complexity comparable across physical settings

Quantum circuit complexity is often measured by the minimum number of gates needed to prepare a target state from a fixed initial state. Counting starts once the inputs are ready, so equal gate counts can conceal different physical costs. For example, one device may supply a pure ancillary qubit, while another must first reset a qubit in a mixed state to obtain one. RCC treats structural fairness as a physical postulate. The structure each device reliably supplies sets its reference zero point. Before choosing a target, fix which controls are available and what each costs. On the device that needs a reset, charge it to the preparation. To compare devices, specify the resources supplied by each background and express the charged operations on a common calibrated cost scale.

Final-state data give a rigorous lower bound on optimal circuit complexity

With the model, cost rules and required accuracy fixed, optimal quantum circuit complexity is the infimum of the costs of all circuits that successfully prepare the target. Each such circuit must generate the structure the target requires beyond what the reference already supplies. A measurement outcome that is common in the target and rare under the reference can certify a cost below which every circuit in the model falls short of the required accuracy.

Research tasks

  • Build a finite-control model for RCC certification. Describe your setup in terms of its reference state, available quantum channels and control rules. Once you verify its reference bound, you can use that bound for different targets in the same model.
  • Certify a lower bound on optimal circuit complexity. Rule out circuits below the certified cost for your target and tolerance. Use an exact spectrum or plan a measurement and calculate the bound from counts. In the graph-state example, the same shot budget gives different bounds depending on the measurement settings.
  • Compare preparation strategies. Check which programs reach the target within tolerance. For a program attaining the upper bound, the gap to the lower bound gives its maximum remaining saving. In the cooling study, a shorter program reaches the full three-qubit target within the chosen tolerance and attains the model’s lower bound.
  • Analyze pure-state complexity with window RCC. Compare pure states with the same global RCC value to see how their complexity is distributed across subsystems. The same analysis applies to mixed states. Use density matrices to track local and correlation contributions along a preparation, or use measurement counts to bound the difference between two states in the measured window.
  • Share a calculation for independent verification. Send a colleague one bundle containing the original inputs and results so they can recompute and verify the calculation independently.
  • Reproduce the paper's reference calculations. Run python -m rcc_refcert reproduce --check to reproduce the bundled cases. Three MATCH results confirm agreement with the frozen expectations, data and report. The paper-to-code map connects the cases to the paper's equations.

Run and share a calculation

With Python 3.10 or newer, install the 0.4.0 source and run the four-qubit reset task in a new working directory.

python -m pip install https://github.com/yeruciwenrou-dotcom/rcc-refcert/archive/3f4788e739df3acc28ada0cf6c5484c14a398af1.zip
python -m rcc_refcert cost template cyclic-reset > task.json
python -m rcc_refcert cost analyze task.json --bundle task.rccbundle

At the default trace-distance tolerance of 1/10, the result is [5,5] atomic slots. The model rules out shorter programs, and a five-slot program reaches the target with halt included. Change epsilon in task.json to try another tolerance and choose a new bundle filename for the next run. Verify the saved calculation with the following command.

python -m rcc_refcert bundle verify task.rccbundle

New in 0.4.0. Plan the shots needed to test a preparation-cost threshold, or use measured histograms to bound the difference in RCC between two states in the same classical measurement window. Full changes and compatibility notes.

Interpreting the results

Exact diagonal-preserving models can bracket the optimal preparation cost between a rigorous lower bound and the cost of a successful program. For general matrix models, the numerical checks give each candidate's cost and trace distance from the target. Window RCC compares state-side complexity at a fixed reference and control bandwidth. A finite-accuracy lower bound on preparation cost also uses the model parameters and one-shot corrections. The scientific scope explains the quantities and their units.
notes: If you use this software in your research, please cite the software version used and the associated RCC paper.
